results.title: NVIDIA B200 Rental Rates Spike 30% as “Insatiable” Demand Takes Hold | TIKR.com
highlights:
The bear case on NVIDIA (NVDA) goes like this: AI tokens get cheaper, GPU rents fall with them, and returns on all that Nvidia hardware shrink.

So far, the rental market isn’t cooperating.

Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal asked on X whether GPU rental rates are “a more useful signal” than token indices. He was replying to Warren Pies, who had just posted: “B200 rental rates up 30% YTD.”

In a follow-up post, Pies called B200 demand “insatiable,” with availability at 0% in his own index.

If companies renting out Nvidia chips earn more per GPU than a year ago, that cuts right against the bear case.

...

Tight supply should mean pricing power for the chipmaker itself. Gross margin is the place to check.

...

Gross margin reached 75% in fiscal 2025 and slipped to about 71% last year. That’s still far above the 57% Nvidia posted just three years ago, so the pricing power is holding up.

Analysts’ forecasts tell the story from another angle.

...

Nebius plans to raise prices next week, and a JPMorgan upgrade flagging rising compute pricing sent Nebius up 6% on the day.

### Here’s the catch

Pies said Fidelity’s Jurrien Timmer is “focusing on older, less consequential, GPUs (A100, H100).” That split raises a fair question. Is the B200 squeeze a lasting trend, or a short scarcity window for the newest chip that closes once supply catches up?

...

If rents keep climbing and estimates keep rising, today’s multiple suggests the market isn’t fully pricing that in. But if B200 rents follow older chips lower, those estimates could come down with them.

results.title: Price Is Not Cost — Understanding AI in a Month — Understanding Machine
highlights:
The first is that a price tells you the cost. It doesn't. Silicon Data publishes a daily index of what it costs to rent one of NVIDIA's H100 chips for an hour. Last December, by the firm's own account, H100 rentals were two dollars an hour. On the twenty-eighth of September its index for the specialist AI cloud providers read two dollars seventy-two. Same chip, nine months older. What the sellers describe is demand running ahead of supply. CoreWeave's chief executive told investors in August that its near-term capacity was effectively sold out, and that prices for older generations of chips were at or above where they were years ago. A price is what someone will pay today. A cost starts with what was paid, spread over the years since.

...

The price is a separate decision, and scarcity moves it. In April the International Energy Agency reported a shortage of the high-bandwidth memory that AI chips need, which it expects to last until at least the end of twenty twenty-seven. Scarce parts raise the cost of building: Microsoft told investors in July that its spending included the impact of higher component pricing. Scarce capacity raises the price of renting. Nothing makes the two move together, which is how a price can sit far above its cost, or below it.

...

It does not, and the clearest evidence is a price that rose while the thing being priced aged. Silicon Data publishes a daily index of the hourly rental price of NVIDIA's H100 accelerator, drawn from "observations across neo-cloud providers, hyperscalers, colocation markets, and private rental platforms", with separate readings for neoclouds and for the hyperscalers, whose on-demand rates are far higher ($7.19 on 28 September 2026). By the firm's account its H100 index rose from $2.00 on 9 December 2025 to $2.20 on 6 January 2026, a jump it called "startling"; the neocloud reading stood at $2.72 on 28 September 2026. The chips being priced are the same model, older each month.

Figure 2. Hourly rental price of an NVIDIA H100, as reported by Silicon Data

Table view

| Date and series | USD per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- |
| 9 Dec 2025 (blog; segment not stated) | 2$ |
| 6 Jan 2026 (blog; segment not stated) | 2.2$ |
| 28 Sep 2026 (neocloud index, SDH100RT) | 2.7$ |

Sources: Silicon Data, 'H100 Price Spike', blog, January 2026 (readings of 9 December 2025 and 6 January 2026; the blog does not name the segment, and its level is consistent with the neocloud series rather than the hyperscaler one); Silicon Data H100 Rental Price Index page, neocloud reading as of 28 September 2026, read 29 September 2026. The page's dated daily series reads $2.60 on 22 September and $2.72 on 28 September; an undated answer in the page's FAQ gives $2.53. The first two readings are the firm's own description of its H100 index and are not identified as the same series as the third.

The sellers explain the rise as demand outrunning supply. Michael Intrator, CoreWeave's chief executive, told investors on 11 August 2026 that "Pricing and margins for our Blackwell and Vera Rubin SKUs are setting new highs while pricing for prior generation SKUs is at or above where it was years ago. Our near-term capacity remains effectively sold out." Nebius attributed its second-quarter pricing to "increasing prices for new-generation GPUs and more than 30% higher pricing on older-generation GPUs versus Q1". The sellers read higher rental prices as a sign of scarce capacity. The prices themselves do not reveal what the chips cost when they were bought, nor whether renting them is profitable, which depends on that cost and on how many hours are sold.

...

The inputs to AI hardware are themselves scarce. The IEA's April update says that "a shortage of high-bandwidth memory – integral to AI chip production – has developed over the past six months and is anticipated to persist through at least the end of 2027". NVIDIA's quarterly report for the period to 26 July 2026 records that it raised its supply commitments "from $ 119 billion last quarter to $ 279 billion", commitments that are "primarily memory and manufacturing facilities". Microsoft's chief financial officer, Amy Hood, told investors on 29 July 2026 that its $41bn of quarterly capital expenditure included "the impact from higher component pricing". The electrical equipment is scarce too: Wood Mackenzie reported in October 2025 that lead times for power transformers had eased to an average of 128 weeks.

Scarcity therefore works on both sides of the ledger at once, but not symmetrically. Dear memory raises what a new data centre costs to build; scarce capacity raises what an existing one can charge. A company whose chips were bought before the squeeze can price at today's rate on yesterday's cost; one buying now pays today's cost and depends on tomorrow's price. That asymmetry, rather than any single number, is what makes a price per megawatt so hard to read.

results.title: GPU rental prices are going up, not down. | Peter Lee
highlights:
GPU rental prices are going up, not down.

Nebius raises rates October 1 — its second hike in three months:
• H100: +17%
• H200: +20%
• B200: +19%
• B300: +21%

Wall Street just split wide open on what it means. JPMorgan upgraded CoreWeave to Overweight ($125 target): pricing power, not debt, is the story — short-term compute now sells at a steep premium, some rivals at ~3x long-term rates.

Days earlier, Rothschild & Co Redburn initiated both CoreWeave and Nebius at Sell, calling neocloud earnings "cyclically inflated."
Both can't be right about durability. But both agree on the present: compute is a seller's market.

Behind the curtain, input costs keep climbing. Mainstream DDR4 closed at $46.11 on Sept 24 (TrendForce) — roughly 4x late-2025 levels — and HBM is effectively sold out for 2026. Memory, not GPUs, is the binding constraint on new capacity.

If you buy compute: review your rate card before Q4 renewals. The "GPU prices only fall" assumption is broken for now — and long-dated fixed-price contracts just flipped from hedge to liability.
Is this pricing power durable, or cyclical?
#FinOps #GPU #AIInfrastructure

results.title: GPU Cloud Economics: What a GPU-Hour Really Costs — Tom's Tech Solutions
highlights:
The 2025 consensus was that GPU-hour prices would keep sliding as Blackwell shipped and Hopper aged. That's not what happened. H100 contract prices went up in 2026, neoclouds raised tens of billions in debt, and the whole business turned into a question of financing. Here's how a GPU-hour actually pencils out.

TL;DR

- SemiAnalysis's H100 one-year contract index went from ~$1.70/hr (Oct 2025) to ~$2.35/hr (Mar 2026), about +40%, as capacity sold out (SemiAnalysis). The GetDeploying on-demand median was ~$3.39 in mid-September (Akash / GetDeploying).
- Scotiabank's model of a 100 MW GB200 NVL72 campus costs $40.3M per MW all-in and needs ~$2.91/GPU-hr for a 15% levered equity IRR. Cash opex is only ~$0.52/hr (Scotiabank via investingLive).
- At CoreWeave in 2Q26, depreciation ate 54% of revenue and interest another 25% (CoreWeave 2Q26). This is a capital-recovery business wearing a cloud costume.

...

The Akash/GetDeploying tracker shows how spread out "the price of an H100" really is. In September it ranged from ~$2 to ~$12 per GPU-hour on demand: specialist clouds at $2–4, AWS P5 around $6.88, Azure's 8-GPU ND H100 v5 around $12.29 (Akash, Sep 12 2026). Spot and multi-year reserved run about half of on-demand.

The direction matters more than the spread, though. Hopper was supposed to fade. Instead, contract rates rose ~40% in five months because on-demand capacity sold out and anyone holding reservations kept them. When the previous-generation GPU gets more expensive, demand is outrunning deployable supply, and that's mostly a power and memory story (see HBM).

results.title: Aethir on GPU Resale Value and Rental Pricing | Aethir
highlights:
## Key Takeaways

1. The first industrial GPU fleets are aging out: Accelerators bought at scale in 2023 and 2024 are approaching the end of their premium service life at roughly the same time.
2. The GPU resale sector: An institutional venue for used and surplus accelerators opened in July 2026, quoting request volumes from hundreds of units to tens of thousands.
3. Aging GPU resale value: Once used GPU pricing is observable, depreciation schedules can be measured against something.
4. The same floor becomes a ceiling on rent: An owner who can sell a card for a known figure won’t rent it below its carrying cost, and a buyer who can see that figure won’t pay far above it.
5. The second-hand GPU market: A market with liquid second-hand supply prices very differently from one where every accelerator is either new or scrapped.

...

An eight-GPU H100 server was trading in the $150,000 to $180,000 range used, against roughly $500,000 for a new B300 system, while H100 rental rates had already fallen from $7 to $10 an hour at launch to $2 to $4. 

Used and refurbished are separate products with separate buyers, and the gap between them is testing and warranty. Secondary-market request volume focuses on H100 and A100 GPUs, which is exactly what you would expect from buyers who want cost per token rather than peak throughput. Inference economics is setting used GPU pricing.

...

The institutional support for the secondary enterprise GPU market arrived in July 2026, when a marketplace for used, refurbished, and surplus accelerators opened alongside an existing reserved-capacity venue, quoting used H100 units at $6,000 to $22,000 against $25,000 to $40,000 new, and used A100 80GB cards at $4,000 to $9,000 against $7,000 to $15,000 new. Equipment in that channel was described as selling 40% to 60% below original list.

The listed inventory across H100, H200, B200, A100, L40S and V100 parts is what a two-sided market looks like from the outside, with several generations quoted at once and buyers choosing hardware by workload.

Operators refreshing on a fixed cadence create predictable supply, which lets a buyer plan around the channel. Hardware liquidity depends far more on that regularity than on any single large disposal.

...

If a used accelerator has a known sale price, the cost of continuing to own it is knowable too, and an owner will rent it out above that carrying cost to earn profits. At the same time, a renter who can price the alternative refuses to pay far above it. GPU rental pricing for older parts gets bracketed from both directions.

New supply keeps pushing the bracket down. NVIDIA said Rubin-based products would reach partners in the second half of 2026, and each generation shifts the previous generation GPU fleet into the value tier. Aethir has tracked why headline compute costs keep rising even as older capacity gets cheaper, which is the same split viewed from the buyer side.

A major discount on last-generation capacity is a signal: When a provider cuts older parts hard, it usually means the fleet is turning over, and the older tier has to earn its keep against a resale quote. GPU fleet turnover shows up in pricing before it shows up in any announcement.

A forward curve for pricing GPUs: Exchange-listed contracts referencing hourly rental indices for the H100 and the B200 mean the older and newer tiers can be priced against each other on a screen. 

Contract term is the exposure: A three-year commitment on previous-generation GPU capacity is a bet that the bracket holds. Axe Compute structured its $260 million cluster of 2,304 NVIDIA B300 GPUs as a 36-month take-or-pay agreement, and pairing a term with an asset life is the whole discipline.

...

A market with liquid second-hand supply behaves differently from one where every accelerator is either new or scrapped, and the difference lands on buyers as optionality. With Gartner forecasting worldwide AI spending to grow 47% in 2026, the volume of workloads that could run perfectly well on last-generation parts keeps growing rapidly.

results.title: AI infrastructure and data center market conditions: AI token spending accelerated sharply in September, while GPU rental and memory pricing gave mixed signals | Report Interpretation | Hilo Research
highlights:
J.P. Morgan reports strong OpenRouter token-volume and spending growth, supporting continued AI infrastructure demand. GPU rental rates fell for A100s and H100s while B200 pricing recovered modestly, and memory spot-price momentum stalled.

...

J.P. Morgan’s September Data Center Watch argues that AI infrastructure demand remains strong based on accelerating LLM token activity, although GPU-rental and memory-spot-price data were less uniformly supportive. The tracker uses a monthly snapshot of roughly 300 models on OpenRouter. Token volume rose 71% month over month, accelerating from 47% in August and 18% in July, and was 30x higher year over year. Token spending increased 28% month over month, versus 7% growth in both August and July, and reached 14x year-over-year growth. The report attributes the volume acceleration primarily to open-weight models: their volume increased 83% month over month and 101x year over year, compared with 39% month-over-month and 10x year-over-year growth for closed-weight models. The report distinguishes average token pricing from volume-weighted pricing. Average pricing rose 4% month over month and 20% year over year, helped by the addition of more expensive image models. However, volume-weighted pricing fell 25% month over month and 55% year over year because demand shifted toward newer, cheaper high-volume models and because some existing models saw price reductions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash added about 41 trillion tokens, or 30% of total volume, at prices below the prior open-weight-model average. Same-model price compression in Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, and GPT-5.6 Sol also contributed. The five largest models represented more than 53% of volume and 50% of spending, but only Tencent’s Hy4 preview appeared in both top-five rankings, illustrating that usage leadership and spending leadership differed. GPU rental pricing for non-hyperscaler capacity was mixed. A100 prices averaged $1.59 per GPU-hour, down 2.8% month over month, while H100 prices averaged $2.64 per GPU-hour, down 2.6%. In contrast, B200 rental prices rose 1.3% month over month to $5.70 per GPU-hour after August’s 1.5% decline. The B200-to-H100 rental-price ratio increased to 2.16x from 2.08x in August, while the H100-to-A100 ratio edged up to 1.66x from 1.65x. J.P. Morgan therefore characterizes compute-rental signals as mixed rather than uniformly strengthening. Memory spot-price momentum also paused. DDR5 16Gb spot pricing declined 1% month over month to $49.70 after five consecutive monthly increases, though it remained 614% above September 2025’s $6.96. NAND 1Tb pricing was effectively unchanged month over month, rising 0.1% to $30.54, but remained 470% above the $5.36 level a year earlier. These figures show that year-over-year memory pricing remained elevated even as month-over-month momentum weakened in September.

...

The report interprets accelerating token volume and spending as evidence that AI infrastructure demand remains strong. At the same time, falling A100 and H100 rental prices and stalled month-over-month memory pricing indicate that pricing conditions across infrastructure inputs were not uniformly tightening.

results.title: Data center GPU price: published rates, dates and sources
highlights:
In short

A data center GPU has no single price: an H100 rents at $5.191 per accelerator-hour on AWS Capacity Blocks, $3.99 per GPU-hour on Lambda, and $2.82 on the SemiAnalysis market index (April 2026). This guide separates list, street and contract price and shows which vendors publish none.

...

Key takeaways

- AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks lists an H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions; a B200 is $12.355; AWS has announced new rates from 7 October 2026.
- Lambda rents an on-demand H100 SXM at $3.99 per GPU-hour; 1-Click Clusters run $6.16 at 16 GPUs down to $5.54 at 256.
- H100 1-year rental contracts rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026, per SemiAnalysis.
- On-demand H100 capacity has been marked sold out on the SemiAnalysis index from February to April 2026.

...

Three published figures answer the question as of 23 September 2026, each from a different price layer. AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML lists the NVIDIA H100 at $5.191 per accelerator-hour in US regions and the B200 at $12.355 per accelerator-hour, with new reservation rates announced effective 7 October 2026 [1]. Lambda lists an on-demand H100 SXM instance at $3.99 per GPU-hour and a B200 SXM6 at $6.69 per GPU-hour [2]. The SemiAnalysis H100 spot-contract composite index, a weighted mean of observed rental prices across the market, stood at $2.82 per GPU-hour in April 2026 [3].

...

Over the past year the contract layer moved sharply upward. SemiAnalysis reports H100 one-year rental contract pricing rising almost 40 percent, from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per GPU-hour by March 2026, with on-demand rental capacity sold out across all GPU types in early 2026 [4]. Those are point figures from the launch article; the same firm's index history publishes the one-year term as a 25th-75th percentile range, which ran $1.45-2.00 in November 2025 and widened to $2.10-2.70 in April 2026, with the on-demand H100 row marked sold out from February through April 2026 [3]. The two starting figures are not in conflict: one is a survey-based point estimate, the other a percentile band from the scraped-market index.

results.title: Nvidia B200 Price Hits $8.01/Hr as GPU Costs Diverge
highlights:
Renting a Nvidia B200 by the hour has no single market price, because Nvidia does not sell it by the GPU-hour and each cloud sets its own rate. Listings in November 2026 reportedly run from $4.11 per GPU-hour, the lowest listed on-demand rate, at Beam Cloud to $16.11 per GPU-hour. Google Cloud listed $16.11 on demand in us-west1 on November 6. Treat any single average, including one quoted from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, as a snapshot to check against provider pages. The B200 is listed as available for rental across multiple cloud providers as of November 6, 2026, and its status is active. It is no longer the only Blackwell option: HGX B300 systems based on Blackwell Ultra became generally available on Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped deployments on October 20, 2026, and Vera Rubin NVL72 is marked early access. Older B200 snapshots, H100 and H200 prices, and any one provider’s rate should not be read as the current market-wide B200 price. Check each provider’s current terms before you commit.

...

The core data point comes from the SemiAnalysis GPU pricing index, which tracks day-to-day cloud rental rates across a basket of providers. In late September 2026, that index put B200 rental pricing at $8.01 per GPU-hour, a 79% climb from where it sat three months earlier. That figure is a market average rather than a price Nvidia publishes or any single provider charges, and a separate October 2026 report from Uvik put B200 median rental pricing at $8.19/GPU-hour across 9 providers, a similar level measured a different way. The same analysis calculated that a B200 now costs 21% more per unit of compute than an H100, a full reversal from June 2026, when a B200 was actually 18% cheaper than an H100 on the same compute-adjusted basis.

...

| GPU | Generation | HBM Memory | Cloud Rental (per GPU-hour) | Indicative Hardware Price | Approx. Cost per GB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | Hopper | 80 GB HBM3 | Baseline (index reference) | ~$31,000 | ~$387.50/GB |
| H200 | Hopper | 141 GB HBM3e | ~1.76x H100 rate | ~$39,999 | ~$283.68/GB |
| B200 | Blackwell | 180 GB HBM3e | $8.01/hr (+21% vs H100 compute-adjusted) | ~$50,000–$70,000 | Not listed |

Two things stand out. First, per-gigabyte pricing across all three chips has converged into a fairly tight band, somewhere around $260 to $390 per gigabyte of HBM, regardless of which generation the memory sits on. Second, the B200’s wide hardware price range ($50,000 to $70,000) reflects a supply-constrained market where list price means less than what a buyer can actually secure, and when, a pattern visible as far back as August 2025, when Northflank reported OEM quotes of $45,000 to $50,000 per B200 GPU and said fully built 8xB200 servers were already exceeding $500,000.

...

Large language models with long context windows need memory to hold the key-value cache during inference. Bigger batch sizes, needed to keep GPU utilization high and serve more users per chip, also eat memory before they eat compute. A model that technically fits on an H100’s 80 GB of HBM3 might only run a handful of concurrent requests before hitting a memory wall, while the same model on a B200’s 180 GB has room to serve far more traffic per chip. That gap is why renters are willing to pay a premium for memory capacity even when the underlying compute-per-dollar math looks worse.

...

None of this happens in a vacuum. High-bandwidth memory production is concentrated among a small number of suppliers, and 2026 has been a year of persistent HBM tightness across the entire AI hardware stack. Nvidia’s own next-generation Rubin Ultra platform has reportedly had to trim memory allocation per package because of the same shortage, and cloud providers including Nebius have already raised prices to reflect higher input costs on memory-heavy configurations. When the memory that feeds B200 and H200 packages is scarce and expensive to source, that cost gets passed straight through to the hourly rental rate. Nvidia itself has acknowledged the squeeze: on October 21, 2026, it announced plans with supply-chain partners to expand manufacturing capacity for AI infrastructure, citing extraordinary demand and constrained capacity.

...

The $8.01 ... In October 2026, Cloud-GPUs tracked B200 availability across 14 providers in 27 countries and listed B200 spot rates at $3.95 to $8.75/GPU-hour, while GPU Economy listed Google Cloud’s B200 spot rate at $1.45/hour. In November 2026, Modal listed B200 at $6.25/GPU-hour, Lambda listed an 8×B200 instance at $6.69/GPU-hour, and Runpod Secure Cloud listed B200 at $7.99/GPU-hour.
